points.point: The Great Stink was an event in July and August 1858 in which hot weather worsened the smell of untreated human waste and industrial effluent on the banks of the Thames, caused by an ageing, inadequate sewer system that emptied directly into the river.
Miasma was believed to spread disease, and three cholera outbreaks before the Great Stink were blamed on the river's problems, so the smell and fears of its effects prompted action by authorities.

Authorities accepted Joseph Bazalgette's proposal for interconnecting sewers sloping eastwards to outfalls beyond the metropolitan area, with work on the Northern and Southern Outfall Sewers lasting from 1859 to 1875 and pumping stations built to lift sewage.

Bazalgette's work ended sewage dumping on the Thames shores and the cholera outbreaks, is thought to have saved more lives than any other Victorian official's efforts, still operates for a city of over nine million, and Peter Ackroyd argues he should be considered a hero of London.
London's old system was inadequate: by 1856 there were around 200,000 cesspits and 360 sewers, some cesspits leaked explosive gases, and many sewers were in poor repair.

Water improvements, flushing toilets, population growth from under one million to three million and industrial outfalls sent far more waste into the sewers, much of which overflowed or discharged directly into the Thames.

John Snow proposed water-borne transmission of cholera, which got little attention at first, but in 1854 removing the Broad Street pump handle was followed by fewer deaths, and a leaking sewer was later found near the well.

Bazalgette's 1856 plan used local sewers feeding larger ones into main outflow pipes, with Northern and Southern Outfall Sewers and pumping stations across high, middle and low-level areas, and it allowed for a population of 4.5 million.
Dry weather lowered the Thames and left raw sewage on its banks, producing the Great Stink, which was so foul that Queen Victoria and Prince Albert cut short a river cruise.
By June the stench disrupted Parliament, where curtains were soaked in lime chloride without success and moving government to Oxford or St Albans was discussed.

Disraeli tabled a bill giving the MBW responsibility for cleaning the Thames, allowing it to borrow £3 million repaid by a levy over forty years, which favoured Bazalgette's 1856 plan; it passed on 2 August, with The Times saying the stench compelled Parliament to act.

Bazalgette's plan for 1,100 miles of street sewers feeding 82 miles of main sewers was put out to tender from 1859 to 1865, and low-lying areas required sewage to be lifted to higher sewers that drained by gravity.

From 1864 Bazalgette built the Victoria, Albert and Chelsea Embankments along the Thames to carry the low-level sewers, reclaiming over 52 acres of land and, in the case of the Victoria Embankment, easing road congestion.

The 1866 cholera outbreak in the East End, which killed 5,596 people in an area not yet connected to Bazalgette's system, was traced to the East London Water Company's contaminated water, which established that cholera was water-borne rather than spread by miasma, and it was London's last outbreak.

Historians and obituarists praised Bazalgette highly, with Doxat saying he probably saved more lives than any other Victorian official, The Times crediting the sewer with adding some 20 years to Londoners' life chances, and Ackroyd placing him among London's heroes.
